healthcareSystem: Universal (National Health Insurance — primarily for residents, tourists pay out-of-pocket)
qualityNotes: World-class healthcare with advanced technology. English availability is limited outside major cities. Most hospitals require upfront payment.
pharmacyHours: Most pharmacies open 9am-8pm; 24/7 pharmacies available in major cities like Tokyo
pharmacyTips: Look for ドラッグスト (drugstores) like Matsumoto Kiyoshi or Cocokara Fine. Pharmacists rarely speak English — bring a translation app. Prescription medicines are dispensed at the pharmacy counter, not sold freely.
prescriptionRules: Most medications require a Japanese prescription. Foreign prescriptions are NOT accepted. Bring all medications you may need in their original packaging.

restrictedMeds.name: Pseudoephedrine (Sudafed and similar)
restrictedMeds.note: Stimulant-based cold medicines containing pseudoephedrine are prohibited. Products like Sudafed, Contac, and similar are illegal to bring into Japan.

restrictedMeds.name: Adderall/amphetamines (ADHD medications)
restrictedMeds.note: Strictly prohibited even with a valid foreign prescription. Includes Adderall, Vyvanse, Dexedrine, and Ritalin/methylphenidate.

restrictedMeds.name: Codeine-containing medications
restrictedMeds.note: Codeine is a controlled substance. Small quantities may be allowed with a doctor's note and Yakkan Shoumei certificate, but many forms are restricted.

restrictedMeds.name: Medical cannabis
restrictedMeds.note: Cannabis in any form is illegal in Japan, including CBD products containing any THC.

restrictedMeds.name: Sleep aids containing flurazepam or similar
restrictedMeds.note: Some benzodiazepines are controlled. Bring documentation if needed.

bringDocumentation: Carry a doctor's letter in English listing all medications and their generic names. For quantities exceeding 1 month's supply, obtain a Yakkan Shoumei (import certificate) from Japan's Pharmaceutical Affairs Agency before arrival. Keep medications in original packaging.

travelInsurance.tips: Japanese hospitals often require upfront payment (cash or credit card). Travel insurance with direct billing and medical evacuation coverage is highly recommended. National Health Insurance does NOT cover tourists.

recommended: Japanese Encephalitis (for rural stays, especially during summer months)
vaccinations.notes: No mandatory vaccinations for travelers from the US or most countries. Ensure routine vaccinations are up to date.

waterNotes: Tap water is safe to drink throughout Japan. Bottled water is also widely available.
foodSafetyTips: Japan has very high food safety standards. Raw fish (sushi/sashimi) is safe at reputable restaurants. Street food is generally safe. Be cautious with consumption of wild mushrooms or unfamiliar plants.
medicalTourismNote: Japan is known for advanced medical technology and excellent cancer treatment. Medical tourism is growing, though costs can be high without insurance.
sources: Japan Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare
metaDescription: Complete health & medication guide for traveling to Japan. Emergency numbers (119/110), pharmacy tips, restricted medications (Sudafed, Adderall banned), vaccination requirements, and travel insurance advice.

hospitals.name: St. Luke's International Hospital
hospitals.notes: Full international department. Major credit cards accepted.

hospitals.name: Tokyo Midtown Medical Center
hospitals.notes: Walk-in clinic for travelers. Popular among expats.

hospitals.name: Osaka International Clinic
hospitals.notes: English-first clinic for tourists and expats.

hospitals.notes: One of Japan's top-ranked hospitals. International patient services.

dentalCare.availability: Excellent dental care available in major cities. Many dental clinics in Tokyo and Osaka have English-speaking dentists.
dentalCare.costRange: ¥3,000-10,000 ($20-70) for a basic consultation; ¥10,000-50,000 ($70-350) for fillings or extractions
dentalCare.notes: Japanese dental care is technically excellent. International clinics in Tokyo (Tokyo Dental Clinic, Mori Dental) cater to English speakers.
dentalCare.emergencyTip: For dental emergencies, visit a hospital emergency department. Most dental clinics are closed on Sundays and holidays. Call the Tokyo Medical Information Service at 03-5285-8181 for referrals.

mentalHealth.englishTherapists: Available in Tokyo and Osaka through TELL (Tokyo English Life Line) and international clinics. Expect ¥10,000-25,000 per session.
mentalHealth.notes: Mental health services in English are limited outside major cities. TELL offers phone and in-person counseling. Many international clinics in Tokyo have psychiatrists.

accessibilityInfo.overview: Japan has good accessibility infrastructure, especially in major cities. Trains, stations, and public buildings are generally wheelchair accessible.
accessibilityInfo.hospitalAccess: Major hospitals are wheelchair accessible with accessible restrooms. International hospitals have multilingual accessibility support.
accessibilityInfo.transport: JR trains and major subway lines have elevators and priority seating. Accessible taxis (UD taxis) available in Tokyo. Wheelchair ramps at most stations.
accessibilityInfo.tips: Request accessible rooms in advance. The Japan Accessible Tourism Center (accessible-japan.com) provides detailed guides. Sidewalks in older areas may have obstacles.

covidStatus.entryRequirements: No COVID testing or vaccination requirements for entry as of 2026.
covidStatus.maskPolicy: Masks are no longer required but remain common in healthcare settings and crowded trains. Many Japanese people continue to wear masks voluntarily.
covidStatus.testing: PCR tests available at clinics and airports. Cost: ¥15,000-30,000 ($100-200) at private clinics.
covidStatus.notes: Japan lifted all COVID entry restrictions in 2023. Healthcare facilities may still require masks.

insuranceClaimProcess: Japanese hospitals typically require upfront payment. Keep all receipts (ryoshusho) and ask for an English medical certificate (shindan-sho). Many hospitals can provide documentation in English at international departments. File claims with your insurer within 30 days of treatment.
